prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and international trade reshape labour demand, wages and the regional distribution of employment

statement.case_for: B027 asks a large question: why wages and jobs diverge across skill groups and places. It answers with a conceptual framework (skill demand, tasks, the race between education and technology) and with transparent quasi-experimental evidence on import competition and local labour markets. This matches the pairing of new evidence and an explanatory framework that I consider the strongest kind of contribution. The core papers span roughly two decades and have been replicated, extended and contested across countries, so the main findings are tested rather than provisional. The work has also shaped research well beyond labour economics, into trade, public economics and political economy, and it has changed how policymakers think about adjustment costs. Nine of eleven members placed it in their top three, and the colleagues I disagree with on credit still agree on its scientific standing. I treat that agreement only as a prompt to test the attribution arguments, not as evidence of merit. The Autor, Hanson, Katz configuration yields one coherent citation: technology and trade as two sources of shifts in labour demand.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution under the three-laureate cap. Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and is left out, so the trade-shock strand is credited less cleanly than the task and skill-demand strand. Katz's core contribution (skill demand and supply) is a different strand from the China-shock identification, so the citation joins two literatures that some members may see as separate prizes. The task framework also overlaps with Acemoglu's work, and the 2021 and 2023 labour-economics prizes may reduce the marginal case. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects, and their external validity, remain debated.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B027 fourth and would credit Autor, Dorn and Hanson, restricting the prize to the trade-shock core. She notes that the task framework draws on Katz, Levy and Acemoglu, and that the three-name cap forces Katz out.
responses.response: I agree that the China-shock identification is most cleanly credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and that leaving out Dorn is a real cost. I still prefer the Katz version. The question the work answers is why labour demand has shifted against some workers and places, and the skill-demand and education-versus-technology strand is the conceptual backbone of that answer. A trade-shock-only prize would be narrower, and it would lean on the part of the evidence where magnitudes are most contested. I also share your concern about the task-framework overlap. My answer is to keep the citation on labour demand, wages and regional employment and not to cite the task model as a discovery. I would accept the Dorn configuration as a defensible alternative if the Committee wants a narrower citation.

responses.point: Krusell proposes only Autor and Hanson. He argues the core contributions can be separated, notes that Katz also appears under B028, and says the Acemoglu overlap complicates attribution.
responses.response: Katz's presence in B028 does not create a double-counting problem in my configuration, because I propose Chetty, Friedman and Hendren for B028 as an alternative and do not credit Katz there. A two-name award would be cleaner, but it drops the skill-demand and education-technology thread, which gives the trade evidence its interpretive context. I accept that the Acemoglu overlap is unresolved. I do not think it removes Katz and Autor's independent contributions to the skill-premium literature, and I would want the Committee to examine that boundary explicitly. Your reservation about whether the empirical shock papers count as a conceptual advance is fair. I weigh the combination of framework and credible evidence more heavily than the novelty of the identification strategy.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first. He argues that Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of the collateral-amplification mechanism, that the work is mature and was confirmed by 2008, and that the overlap with the 2022 prize is a risk but not disqualifying.
responses.response: On attribution B006 is cleaner than B027, since a Kiyotaki-Moore award has no Dorn-type exclusion, and the mechanism's importance for macro-finance is not in doubt. I weigh it below B027 for two reasons. The mechanism is mostly theoretical, and its direct empirical identification is thinner than for B027, where the main claims have been tested against micro data in many settings. It also sits adjacent to the 2022 financial-crisis prize, which you flag yourself. I do not read your point as undervaluing B027's maturity. The disagreement is over how much weight to put on a clean originator pair versus broader empirical confirmation. I am less sure on that question than on the ranking, and I would not oppose B006 as a laureate set if the Committee prefers its attribution clarity.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B027 first with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He says the China-shock effects are best credited to those three, the task framework has wider authorship including Katz, and omitting Katz is an attribution cost.
responses.response: We agree on scientific merit and on the main attribution risk. We differ on which of the two costs to accept: I give up Dorn, you give up Katz. Your version cleanly credits the trade-shock evidence, but it makes the prize a trade-adjustment award, and the task and skill-demand strand then becomes a footnote. Mine has a broader citation and a harder-to-defend boundary around Dorn. I do not think the profession's judgment of the scientific contribution settles this, and it may be a matter for the wording of the citation. I am happy for the Committee to test both versions against the same criterion: who is most responsible for the central findings the citation names.

uncertainties: Whether the China-shock magnitudes, persistence and external validity are judged robust enough to anchor half of the citation.
How much of the task-framework credit overlaps with Acemoglu's earlier recognised work and with scholars outside the credited names, such as Levy and Murnane.
Whether Dorn or Katz better completes the three-person set, which depends on whether the citation is framed around trade shocks or around labour demand more broadly.
Whether the Committee would regard the technology and trade strands as one achievement or as two separate prizes.
Whether B032 or B028 would be preferable if members judge B027's attribution too contested; B028 faces further maturity doubts raised by several colleagues, which I take seriously.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited in any shortlisted ballot. I work in labour economics, which is close to B027 and B028, but I do not treat that as a connection requiring recusal.
